explanations.explanation: Right there in the verse: “In darkness they do their works…” The whole plan is to hide where nobody can look. It's like sneaking a cookie off the cooling rack with the lights off, then standing there with crumbs on your shirt like it's a secret. Isaiah opens that line with “Woe,” so he's not impressed.

I see why you'd guess it, friend, but Isaiah never puts them in the temple courts. He says “In darkness they do their works…” These folks are digging deep and hiding, and nobody hides in the middle of a busy courtyard. That's like trying to sneak a cookie past a whole crowd.

Fields make sense for a lot of Bible stories, but not this one. Isaiah says “In darkness they do their works…” The text doesn't mention a single field here. Their hiding place is the dark, and they're digging deep to keep their plans hidden.

That's it, baker. They say, “Who sees us, and who will know?” They're acting like the dark makes them invisible. It's like thinking nobody can hear you chewing a cookie because you turned the TV up. Isaiah answers that kind of thinking with “Woe.”

It's True, friend. Isaiah quotes them asking, “Who sees us, and who will know?” Those are the words of people who think nobody is watching. They dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD, and Isaiah answers them with “Woe.”

Clay! Isaiah says it's turned upside down “as if the potter were regarded as clay.” The one doing the shaping gets treated like the lump on the wheel. That's like a cookie telling the oven how to run the timer. It's backwards, and Isaiah says so.

King is a good-sounding word, friend, but it's not what Isaiah says. The verse says “as if the potter were regarded as clay.” The mix-up is about who made whom. The potter forms the pot, and the pot has no business acting like the one in charge.

Servant is close in feel, but Isaiah picks a different word. He says “as if the potter were regarded as clay.” The picture is a maker being treated like the material he works with. Flip that around and you've got things upside down, just like Isaiah says.

Not quite, friend. Isaiah asks, “In a very short time, will not Lebanon become an orchard…” That's a very short time, not a long one. If you pulled a batch out of the oven and it was already cooling on the rack, that would be about the same surprise.
False is right. Isaiah says “In a very short time, will not Lebanon become an orchard, and the orchard seem like a forest?” Very short time. Nobody's checking a calendar for this one.
Hear is right. Isaiah says, “the deaf will hear the words of the scroll…” A scroll is a written document, and words that were silent on it get heard. I think that would be a good day for anybody.

See is right. The verse says, “out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see.” Out of the deep darkness, friend. It makes me think about that line every time I picture a door opening and light coming in.

Speak is a fair guess, but Isaiah doesn't say it here. The verse is about the deaf and the blind, so it says, “the deaf will hear the words of the scroll.” Hearing is what's coming for them. The speaking part isn't in this line.

Singing would be a nice party, baker, but it's not in this verse. Isaiah says the deaf will hear and the blind will see. The line goes, “the deaf will hear the words of the scroll.” Hearing is the word that goes in the blank.

Close is sneaky, friend, but it doesn't fit. Isaiah says “out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see.” Eyes that close would be the opposite of what's promised. These eyes are opening to see.

That's it. Isaiah says, “The humble will increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.” Notice the word increase. Their joy goes up. Whoever is humble gets to enjoy that.

Rest sounds nice, friend, but Isaiah doesn't say it here. The verse says “The humble will increase their joy in the LORD…” The joy is in the LORD, not in a day off. The poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
That's a big promise, but it isn't the one in this verse. Isaiah says “the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.” The joy is in the LORD. Ruling over anybody isn't mentioned here.
Evil is right. Isaiah says “all who look for evil will be cut down.” These are people who go searching for it. It's a strange thing to hunt for when you could be hunting for a dropped chocolate chip.

Peace is a good thing to look for, so I get the guess. But Isaiah says “all who look for evil will be cut down.” The group in this verse is hunting for the wrong thing. Peace isn't what they're after.
Wisdom would be a happier ending, friend, but that isn't the word here. Isaiah says “all who look for evil will be cut down.” Those are the ones in this group. Evil goes in the blank.

Right. Isaiah says they are the ones “who with false charges deprive the innocent of justice.” A charge that isn't true, used to take what an innocent person is owed. I can't make that one funny, baker. It's just heavy, and I think it's meant to be.

Taxes are a sore spot for most of us, friend, but Isaiah doesn't mention them here. The verse says they “with false charges deprive the innocent of justice.” The tool they use is a charge that isn't true. Justice gets taken from the innocent that way.

That sounds dramatic, but there are no soldiers in this verse. Isaiah says they “with false charges deprive the innocent of justice.” These people use accusations that aren't true. It's all about words, which is why the verse starts with those who “indict a man with a word.”

Hold on, friend, it goes the other way. The LORD who redeemed Abraham says, “No longer will Jacob be ashamed and no more will his face grow pale.” That's a promise that the shame stops. Pale faces turn back to normal.

False is right. The LORD says, “No longer will Jacob be ashamed and no more will his face grow pale.” No longer and no more, which is two ways of saying it's done. That's good news for the house of Jacob.
That's the one. The LORD says Jacob sees his children around him, “the work of My hands.” Hands are what a maker uses. I stamp cookies with a mustache, so I take that kind of thing personally.

That's a nice picture, baker, but it isn't what the LORD says in this verse. He calls them “the work of My hands.” These children are something He made, like a potter shaping clay. That ties back to the pot and the potter from earlier in the passage.

Fancy, friend, but the LORD doesn't say that here. The verse calls Jacob's children “the work of My hands.” It's about something He has made, not something He wears. Like a cookie fresh off the rack, it's something that came from the hands that made it.

Honor! The LORD says, “they will honor My name, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and they will stand in awe of the God of Israel.” That's three things in a row. When they see the work of His hands, they respond.

Questioning is what grumbling sounds like, so I see why it came to mind. But the LORD says “they will honor My name.” Honoring is the opposite of poking at it. The same verse says they will stand in awe of the God of Israel.

Forget would be a sad ending, baker, and it isn't the one here. The LORD says, “they will honor My name…” They remember it and hold it high. The verse also says they will stand in awe of the God of Israel.

True! The last line says, “those who grumble will accept instruction.” The grumblers come around. I have grumbled at a oven timer before, and it didn't care one bit. The LORD's words do better with grumblers than that.

It's True, friend. The LORD says, “Then the wayward in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction.” Grumbling doesn't get the last word. They end up accepting instruction.
